title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
content:
## 2.1 Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

### The career logic of FIELDWISE

FIELDWISE is designed around a single, coherent career transition. The fellow enters the action as a plant physiologist and agronomist and leaves it as an Earth-observation and geospatial crop scientist able to work independently on transferable agricultural intelligence. The intended progression is explicit: Plant Physiologist/Agronomist to EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist to Independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. Every training and supervision measure below is aligned to that trajectory, so that skills development is not a generic add-on but the mechanism by which the fellowship changes what kind of researcher — and employee — the fellow becomes. The action is a European Fellowship of 30 months, comprising a 24-month research period hosted at ELTE followed by a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR that supplies the inter-sectoral half of the profile. This structure is deliberate: the academic host builds the scientific and methodological competences, and the non-academic placement builds the operational and sector-facing competences that the host cannot provide, so that the resulting profile is credible both inside and outside academia.

### Skills development: the competence gap and how it is closed

The skills-development plan starts from an honest statement of where the fellow is strong and where she is not. She combines a foundation in agronomy, plant protection and plant physiology with developing expertise in EO, GIS and agricultural data science. FIELDWISE addresses the remaining, well-identified competence gap in Bayesian and probabilistic modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty quantification, domain adaptation and decision evaluation. Because the gap is named precisely, the training content can be matched to it precisely rather than promised in the abstract.

The host-to-fellow training content is correspondingly specific. Through supervised research practice and named ELTE courses the fellow acquires: geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning and domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software and web deployment; and IP and research exploitation. These eleven competences are delivered as supervised practice plus named ELTE courses and are written into the Career Development Plan as concrete training and career needs, not as aspirations. They are exactly the competences the scientific work packages consume, so the fellow learns them by doing the science the proposal is funded to do — the strongest form of postdoctoral skills acquisition.

Critically, the transfer of knowledge is genuinely two-way rather than a one-directional upskilling. The fellow brings to ELTE plant physiology, horticultural crop science, plant protection and agronomy, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping, hyperspectral field measurement, the biological interpretation of Earth-observation signals, and preliminary development of the DrR - Digital Agronomist concept. This bidirectionality — crop physiology and agronomy in exchange for geospatial and data science — is what makes the fellow a bridging researcher at the end of the action rather than a physiologist who has taken some machine-learning courses. It is also the basis of a distinctive and defensible scientific profile: biological understanding combined with scalable geospatial prediction and operational agricultural decision support, a combination that is scarce in either community alone.

Beyond the eleven research competences, the plan develops seven transferable-skill strands: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. These are the competences an independent researcher needs to lead rather than to assist, and they are the competences employers outside academia value as much as inside it. Open science is embedded in the day-to-day work — harmonisation protocols, validation split manifests, hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, analysis and model code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata and open-access publication — so FAIR and open-science literacy are practised on real project outputs rather than taught in isolation.

### Supervision and quality assurance as a development instrument

The supervision arrangements are structured to make skills acquisition monitored and correctable. There is a weekly one-to-one meeting between the fellow and the supervisor, and a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor through the modelling-intensive work packages WP3 (Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction) and WP4 (Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability), tapering to monthly outside that window. A monthly written progress record is held by the fellow, and there is a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors. The co-supervisor provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing, while the fellow designs, builds and runs the models — a division that gives the fellow ownership of the scientific method while ensuring the newest and most demanding competences (probabilistic modelling, uncertainty, validation design) are quality-assured by an expert. This is credible mentoring for exactly the part of the profile that is new to her.

### The Career Development Plan as the carrying instrument

All of the above is made operational, trackable and reviewable through the Career Development Plan (deliverable D1.3, Career Development Plan), owned jointly by the fellow and the supervisor and established jointly by both supervisors and the fellow. It is an early deliverable, agreed by M3, and it carries six components: research objectives (O1 to O6); training and career needs (the eleven host-to-fellow competences delivered as supervised practice plus named ELTE courses); the seven transferable-skill strands; teaching; publications planning; and open-science engagement. It is not a one-off document: it is reviewed at each of the five steering points across the action, and its progress is itself a tracked key performance indicator — the plan is to be agreed by M3 and reviewed at all five steering points. Attaching a KPI to the plan means the fellow's development is governed with the same discipline as the scientific deliverables, which is what an evaluator needs to see to believe the career measures are real rather than declaratory. The review point that falls within the placement period ensures that non-academic career development is actively reviewed at precisely the moment it is most in play.

### Employability inside academia

The scientific competences the fellowship builds are directly matched to academic and research-sector demand. By the end of the action the fellow will hold advanced competence in Bayesian and probabilistic modelling, uncertainty quantification, spatio-temporal validation, sensor-domain transfer, cross-country adaptation, operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and IP and exploitation, together with the experience of taking a scientific concept the full length of the pipeline — from experimental evidence to a validated model, to cross-country testing, to commercial-field testing, to a delivered MVP. Very few early-career researchers can demonstrate that end-to-end span. This profile is relevant to European research institutes, universities, EU agricultural and environmental research, and Earth-observation organisations. The teaching measures reinforce the academic track specifically: the fellow co-designs and delivers a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, and co-supervises the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. Teaching is framed not as a competence to be acquired but as an existing strength transferred into a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction — the fellow taught for five years at university level, including syllabus design, lecturing and examining and Bachelor's thesis supervision — with the developmental step being the move to Earth-observation teaching in English at an informatics faculty and the step up from Bachelor's to doctoral-level supervision. This gives the fellow demonstrable, current higher-education teaching experience at the host, which is a concrete asset for an academic appointment.

Publication planning is aligned to the same end. Dissemination targets four principal scientific outputs — physiological and hyperspectral early-warning signatures of processing-tomato water stress; hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling; temporal and cross-country transferability of water-stress models; and research-to-commercial transfer and decision-oriented evaluation of agricultural AI — with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions targeted during or shortly after the fellowship. A first-author publication record on a distinctive topic is the currency of academic progression, and the plan builds it deliberately.

### Employability outside academia

The non-academic placement at AgroVIR is the measure that makes the beyond-academia claim credible rather than asserted. AgroVIR is the non-academic placement host, and the six-month placement is embedded inside the company that operates the commercial farms the project targets. The placement supplies the inter-sectoral half of the career progression — operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and direct exposure to commercial agricultural software requirements — none of which the academic host can provide. It is precisely the segment of the profile that makes the fellow employable in precision-agriculture companies, irrigation-technology companies and farm-management-information-system (FMIS) providers, as well as in academia. The placement work content is deliberately training-oriented rather than service to the company: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; a structured operational assessment of the MVP; authoring an FMIS integration roadmap from inside an implementing company; and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. Each of these is a transferable, sector-recognised competence. The placement is supervised on site by a named senior member of the company's research staff, giving the inter-sectoral training the same mentoring seriousness as the academic period. Because the placement is assessed by evaluators as part of Part B-1, it is presented here as an integral career measure and not merely as a scheduling detail: it converts the fellow's operational-transfer competences from a claim into lived, evidenced experience.

### Contribution of the proposed skills development to the future career

Taken together, the measures produce a researcher whose profile spans a genuine gap in the European research and innovation landscape. The academic period builds the scientific and methodological depth; the placement builds the operational and inter-sectoral breadth; the Career Development Plan governs and reviews both; and the two-way knowledge transfer ensures the fellow ends as a bridging scientist rather than a specialist in one camp. This is a direct instantiation of the MSCA-PF expected outcome of an increased set of research and transferable skills and competences leading to improved employability and career prospects within academia and beyond (EO-01), and of the associated impact of improved researcher employability and career mobility within and beyond academia (EI-01). The international dimension (the Hungary-to-Bulgaria transfer work with MVCRI), the inter-sectoral dimension (the AgroVIR evaluation and placement) and the interdisciplinary dimension (the physiology-to-geoinformatics transfer) also forge the new mind-sets and cross-boundary approaches the programme seeks (EO-02). The credibility of the career case rests on three features an evaluator can check: the competence gap is named precisely and the training is matched to it; the plan carries a tracked KPI and five review points, so development is governed, not merely promised; and the inter-sectoral claim is backed by a real, six-month placement inside a commercial company rather than by assertion. On this basis the proposed measures are well suited to enhancing the fellow's career perspectives and employability across both academic and non-academic destinations.
